work.title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
work.creator: J. K. Rowling

summary: An orphan discovers he is a wizard, finds friends and a school full of wonders, and with them solves the mystery of the Stone and faces Voldemort.

hunger.why: The Dursleys starve Harry in his cupboard, and Hogwarts answers with feasts, the trolley of sweets, and Hagrid's rock cakes.

thirst.why: No character seeks or lacks water.

feeling-cold-hot.why: Winter snow at Hogwarts and the hut on the rock in the storm are brief settings.

sleepiness.why: Night-time wanderings under the invisibility cloak cost sleep, but fatigue is marginal.

curiosity.why: Harry discovers Diagon Alley, Hogwarts' moving staircases, the forbidden corridor, and the Forest; the wizarding world is explored.

explanation-seeking.why: Who is Nicolas Flamel, what is under the trapdoor, and who is trying to steal the Stone drive the plot.

skill-acquisition.why: Harry learns spells, potions, and flying, becomes the youngest Seeker in a century, and Hermione masters every class.

play.why: Quidditch matches, wizard chess, Exploding Snap, and the giant chess game are central pleasures.

resource-accumulation.why: Harry's Gringotts gold, the Weasleys' poverty, and the Stone that makes gold matter but do not drive the plot.

resource-foraging.why: Shopping for wands and robes in Diagon Alley and the hunt for the Stone involve gathering what is needed.

mental-time-travel.why: The trio plan how to pass Fluffy and the obstacles, and Harry gazes at his lost family in the Mirror of Erised.

fear-of-predators.why: The three-headed dog Fluffy, the mountain troll, Devil's Snare, and the hooded thing drinking unicorn blood threaten the children.

fear-of-aggressors.why: Voldemort through Quirrell, Malfoy's bullying, and the Dursleys' cruelty are human threats throughout.

fear-of-heights.why: Neville falls from his broom, Harry's broom is jinxed high above the pitch, and the fall through the trapdoor is a plunge.

disgust.why: Troll bogies on Harry's wand, Dudley's pig tail, and the slaughtered unicorn's silver blood evoke revulsion.

pain-aversion.why: Harry's scar burns near Quirrell, Neville breaks his wrist, and Quirrell's hands blister at Harry's touch.

pride.why: Harry catches the Snitch, Gryffindor wins the House Cup, and Harry is famed as the Boy Who Lived.

shame.why: Ron is ashamed of hand-me-downs, Neville of his clumsiness, and Hermione cries after being called a nightmare.

moral-pride.why: Neville stands up to his friends, Harry chooses not Slytherin, and the trio break rules to stop the theft.

guilt.why: Hermione lies to protect the boys and feels the weight of it; remorse is otherwise slight.

warmth.why: Hagrid's kindness, Mrs Weasley's hand-knitted jumper, and Dumbledore's gentleness give Harry his first warmth.

moral-blame.why: The children condemn Malfoy, suspect Snape, and loathe the Dursleys' cruelty; Dumbledore judges Voldemort's evil.

moral-praise.why: Dumbledore publicly awards points for Neville's courage and the trio's bravery, and Harry is celebrated for defeating Voldemort.

revenge.why: Hagrid gives Dudley a pig's tail, and Malfoy plots to get the trio expelled.

forgiveness.why: Ron and Hermione make up after the troll, and Harry excuses Hagrid's slips.

compassion.why: Hermione helps Neville, Hagrid nurses the dragon Norbert, and the trio protect each other.

affiliation.why: Harry meets Ron on the train, wins Hermione after the troll, and is welcomed by Hagrid and the Weasleys.

friendship.why: The bond of Harry, Ron, and Hermione is the heart of the book.

sadness.why: Harry's murdered parents and his longing before the Mirror of Erised carry sorrow.

humor.why: The Weasley twins, Peeves, Dudley's tail, and Ron's jokes keep the tone light.

embarrassment.why: Ron's blushes over poverty, Neville's mishaps, and Harry's awkwardness at his own fame recur.

reasoning.why: Hermione solves Snape's logic puzzle, and the trio argue over whether Snape is the thief.

coalitional-affiliation.why: Gryffindor against Slytherin, the Sorting, and the House Cup make group identity constant.

status-seeking.why: House points, Malfoy's snobbery, Quidditch glory, and Harry's fame create a hierarchy to climb.

envy.why: Dudley's spoiled jealousy, Ron's envy of Harry's fame, and Malfoy's resentment of Harry appear.

anger.why: Harry's fury at Snape and Malfoy, and Uncle Vernon's rage at the letters, are secondary.

hatred.why: Snape's apparent hatred of Harry and Harry's loathing of Malfoy are present but not dominant.

long-term-love.why: Lily and James's love is recalled through Harry's longing.

parental-care.why: Lily's sacrifice protects Harry, the Dursleys neglect him, and Hagrid and Mrs Weasley stand in as guardians.

parental-investment.why: The Dursleys spoil Dudley, the Weasleys raise seven children, and Hogwarts educates the young.

familial-love.why: Harry's longing for his parents, the Weasleys' warmth, and the Dursleys as a hostile family frame the story.
